## Overview

Backpressure in a streaming pipeline is the mechanism by which a slow downstream consumer signals an upstream producer to reduce its emission rate, rather than letting an unbounded buffer grow until the process runs out of memory.

Without backpressure, a fast producer sending data to a slow consumer would accumulate unprocessed items in intermediate buffers, eventually exhausting available memory and causing the application to crash or degrade severely.

## Implementation Approaches

### Bounded Queues with Blocking

The simplest form uses bounded queues that block the producer once full. When the queue reaches its maximum capacity, further `send()` or `enqueue()` operations from the producer block until the consumer drains enough items to make space.

**Characteristics:**
- Synchronous blocking of the producer thread
- Simple to understand and implement
- Can cause thread starvation if buffers fill up

### Credit-Based Flow Control

In credit-based systems, the consumer explicitly grants the producer permission to send N more items (credits). The producer tracks available credits and sends only when credits remain.

**Characteristics:**
- Asynchronous; producer does not block but waits for credits
- Consumer has fine-grained control over concurrency and load
- Requires explicit credit accounting

### Reactive Pull Models

In pull-based (reactive) models, the consumer requests items on its own schedule instead of the producer pushing them. The producer only emits when the consumer signals readiness.

**Characteristics:**
- Inverts the traditional producer–consumer relationship
- Consumer-driven pacing; producer never overstays capacity
- Fits well with functional and reactive programming libraries
